html:
The Papuans are the native peoples of New Guinea and some nearby islands who speak Papuan languages, as opposed to the Austronesian languages of many coastal neighbours. The map shows them from 800 to 1815.

Their ancestors arrived about 50,000 years ago, when New Guinea and Australia were one land. They were among the first farmers in the world: at Kuk Swamp in the highlands they drained gardens for taro and bananas thousands of years ago. The earlier stage of that story is under Papuan neolithic farmers.

New Guinea is the most language-rich place on earth. Papua New Guinea alone has more than 800 languages. Valleys separated by mountains and forest kept groups small and apart. Leaders were often "big men" who won standing by giving feasts and gifts of pigs and shells rather than by birth.

In the last few centuries the sweet potato, an American crop that reached the island after 1500, let highland farmers grow food higher up, and populations rose. Coastal peoples traded with Austronesian neighbours, and bird of paradise plumes went west through the Sultanate of Tidore to markets in Asia. Portuguese and Spanish sailors named the island in the 1500s. The crowded highland valleys stayed unknown to outsiders until gold prospectors reached them in the 1930s. The eastern half later became Papua New Guinea.
sum: The Papuans are the native peoples of New Guinea and some nearby islands who speak Papuan languages, as opposed to the Austronesian languages of many coastal neighbours. The map shows them from 800 to 1815.
